newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah slips on liquidity, Iraq.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah slips on liquidity, Iraq.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah came under pressure on Thursday as ample money market liquidity weighed on domestic interest rates.
"The narrowing of interest rate differentials between the rupiah and the dollar prompted the overseas dollar buying minutes after the open," said a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta.

Dealers said concern about an escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iraq also boosted sentiment for the dollar. Some players were awaiting developments in Thursday's court hearing of a lawsuit filed by ousted opposition leader Megawati Sukarnoputri against the government.

"The market perceives that the West is attacking Moslem states and Indonesia is one of them. I don't think it's a good reason but it's an excuse to buy dollars," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.
She said the central bank's gradual raising of the intervention rate was also keeping the dollar supported on the downside.
Spot rupiah was at 2,346.00/46.50 at midday, compared with an opening of 2,344.50/45.50. The central bank set its intervention rate at 2,342/2,460 and the conversion rate at 2,342/2,388 on Wednesday.
In Thailand, the baht was slightly weaker on some dollar short-covering following the central bank's recent injection of funds into the money market.

The Bank of Thailand injected funds amounting to 22 billion baht into the system on Tuesday and Wednesday to ease tight market liquidity caused by bimonthly corporate tax payments and commercial banks' withholding of funds for the central bank reserve requirement.

"Most banks appeared to have collected sufficient funds for the coming reserve requirement. The central bank's heavy fund injection over the past few days also raised money supply," said a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok.
The Malaysian ringgit lost some ground on commercial sales by a Singapore-based bank, but the currency remained well contained within its recent trading range against the dollar.

"But trading was a bit quiet and I don't think dollar/ringgit will move much today," said one foreign bank dealer. He said many were looking to buy the dollar on dips and this was limiting the downside for the U.S. currency.
A Singapore-based dealer said dollar/ringgit looked set to break above 2.5000 but it would be a slow grind higher.
- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-230 8911), Tang Nguyen in Bangkok (662- 252-9950), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364) and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703092)
